title: Magic transfer in quantum spin chains
authors: Antonio Palamara, Chad Nelmes, Enrico C. Domanti, Francesco Perciavalle
abstract: Quantum communication protocols based on spin chains have been extensively studied, yet their ability to transmit nonstabilizer resources has not been systematically addressed. We investigate the transport of quantum magic in spin chains through the natural dynamics of systems initialized in nonstabilizer states, and quantify the transported resource via the stabilizer norm. We analyze three experimentally feasible state-transfer protocols, ranging from noisy to (quasi-)perfect transfer, including one realizable in trapped-ion platforms. We find that the geometry of the injected state strongly influences transport: states in the lower Bloch hemisphere achieve higher transfer quality, whereas states in the upper hemisphere give rise to an efficient magic transport only beyond a threshold value of the parameter controlling the tendency towards perfect transfer. These features are robust across all protocols and identify the Hamiltonian and state properties that favor high-quality transfer. Moreover, we identify a parameter region, relevant to the initial state preparation, in which the transported magic exceeds the initial encoding, indicating that such spin systems can act as magic-amplification channels. Our results establish the conditions for efficient transport of nonstabilizer resources and demonstrate quantum magic as a sensitive probe of quantum transport beyond population dynamics.
summary: This paper investigates the transport of quantum magic—a specific nonstabilizer resource—through spin chains using the XX Hamiltonian. By analyzing three different state-transfer protocols, the authors demonstrate that the initial state geometry dictates transfer efficiency and reveal a mechanism where the spin chain can actively amplify the injected quantum magic. This establishes a new diagnostic tool for assessing quantum channel capabilities beyond standard fidelity measures.
main_problem: The paper investigates the transport of quantum magic, a nonstabilizer resource, through quantum spin chains, treating it as a distinct problem from standard Perfect State Transfer (PST). It aims to characterize how this resource is preserved and amplified during state transfer.
main_result: The geometry of the initial state significantly influences transport quality, showing an asymmetry where lower-hemisphere states transfer better than upper-hemisphere states. Furthermore, the system can act as a magic-amplification channel when the transported magic exceeds the initial encoding.
method: The analysis uses theoretical modeling based on the XX Hamiltonian and quantifies resource transfer using the stabilizer norm (SN) of the reduced density matrix at various sites and times.
model_or_system: The system is a one-dimensional quantum spin chain governed by an XX Hamiltonian. Three state-transfer protocols are analyzed, interpolating between homogeneous, ballistic, and power-law decaying couplings. The analysis focuses on T-states initialized in the upper or lower Bloch hemisphere.

important_parameters: Interpolation parameter $\alpha$ controlling coupling regimes, initial state geometry (upper vs. lower Bloch hemisphere), and system size $L$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the validity of using the stabilizer norm to quantify nonstabilizerness and assumes specific forms for Hamiltonian interpolation between different transfer limits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how magic transfer depends on the initial state's Bloch hemisphere, show site-dependent SN dynamics across protocols, and plot $D_{	ext{max}}$ versus Hamiltonian parameters ($\alpha$, $\gamma$).
paper_structure: The paper establishes quantum magic transport as a resource problem, analyzes three specific spin chain protocols (A, B, C) using the XX Hamiltonian, derives the evolution of local Bloch vectors, and presents results showing state-geometry dependence and potential for magic amplification.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-local quantum resource transfer in physical systems like trapped ions or superconducting circuits, providing quantitative metrics (SN) beyond simple fidelity to characterize channel quality. The concept of 'magic amplification' suggests novel ways to process quantum information.
